The Electric Prunes - I Had Too Much To Dream (Last Night) (1967)

The Electric Prunes originally formed as The Sanctions at Taft High School in Los Angeles, renaming themselves in 1966. They were introduced to record producer Dave Hassinger, and after a series of rehearsals at Leon Russell's house released a debut single, "Ain't It Hard". Despite its commercial failure, Reprise Records agreed that the band could record a second single.

Convinced that the band could not write their own songs, Hassinger sought material from the professional songwriting team of Annette Tucker and lyricist Nancie Mantz. One of the tunes was "I Had Too Much to Dream (Last Night)", a song that, according to some sources was originally conceived as an orchestral piano ballad. However, according to Tucker, "I came up with the title one day and called Nancie. She loved it and we wrote it the next day in one half hour....The words were there and my melody came easily. I was influenced by the Rolling Stones at the time and that is how I heard that song being recorded....Nancie and I envisioned this as a rock song." A demo version recorded for Hassinger by singer-songwriter Jerry Fuller (in some sources wrongly identified as Jerry Vale), may have been the source of the story of the song's origin as a ballad.

At the time, the Electric Prunes comprised singer James Lowe, lead guitarist Ken Williams, rhythm guitarist James "Weasel" Spagnola, bassist Mark Tulin, and drummer Preston Ritter. The oscillating, reversed guitar which opens the song originated from the rehearsals at Russell's house, where Williams recorded with a 1958 Gibson Les Paul guitar with a Bigsby vibrato unit. According to Lowe, "We were recording on a four-track, and just flipping the tape over and re-recording when we got to the end. Dave cued up a tape and didn't hit 'record,' and the playback in the studio was way up: ear-shattering vibrating jet guitar. Ken had been shaking his Bigsby wiggle stick with some fuzztone and tremolo at the end of the tape. Forward it was cool. Backward it was amazing. I ran into the control room and said, 'What was that?' They didn't have the monitors on so they hadn't heard it. I made Dave cut it off and save it for later."

If you're talking about something like HughesNet, it's garbage. But for some people it's literally their only option.

Used to be, it was downlink only. But now they do have bi-directional service, so you're not stuck at 56kbps for upload. But it's still not optimal. Most plans are in the 1-2mbit range, and are capped worse than any terrestrial service. So you're not going to be streaming or gaming on it.

The worst factor, however, is latency. You're communicating with a satellite in either geosynchronous (orbital period matches the Earth's, but ground-track drifts during the day) or geostationary (same as above, but but they stay over the same spot) orbit.

Those kind of orbits require a lot of altitude. Geostationary is 35,786 kilometers. Speed of light is 299,792.458 kilometers/second. That means round-trip time just between you and the satellite is roughly 239ms. But then the signal has to be bounced to a ground station before going out to the rest of the world. So realistically, the bare minimum you would ever see on a ping is 500ms. One full half second between sending a packet and receiving a reply.

To put that in perspective, most terrestrial internet has latency between 10 and 50ms to some arbitrary server.

Starlink is going online for beta testing soon, and they're promising better. But instead of a few satellites in high orbit, they're going to be using massive swarms of satellites in low orbit (550km or so). Once overhead is taken into account, they're targeting earth-to-satellite times of around 30ms.

So Starlink might turn out to be decent, but you'll have to wait and see. But the current satellite offerings are garbage if you have literally any other option available.

Are you asking about satellite internet because you moved to a rural area?

If so, I can share what my family did when we moved.

There is absolutely no wired internet in our area. As a family of three, we used to burn about 450 GB a month in the suburbs on our unlimited hi speed internet plan.

I looked into satellite, but it wasn't ideal not only because of the slower speeds, but because of major latency issues that arise when connecting to a VPN. My wife must use her VPN for work.

So although we only have one bar of LTE reception on our phones, we decided to use only cellular data. It has been fine.

The first thing we did was upgrade our cell phones to (I think it's called) the Elite plan on AT&T. It has unlimited data on your cellular devices and 30GB of hotspot. When the 30GB of hotspot are depleted, they throttle the hotspot speed but do not charge extra for it.

I added the AT&T Home Internet package, which is another device that provides 100GB of wireless internet. I use this device for my laptop to do some work, and shitpost. I set all my video streaming to standard definition to save on GB. I don't need to watch videos of the riots in HD.

My wife uses a Moxie box that was provided by her work. That's another 100Gb of wireless data. She has had no problems connecting to her VPN. There is a little latency when it comes to Zoom meetings with many participants, but overall, she has no problems with it.

My daughter is only allowed to use her unlimited data on her phone. She has 30GB of hotspot that she uses to connect to her laptop or ipad when she wants to use a different device.

My wife uses her hotspot data to stream TV to her tablet before she goes to bed. I hardly use any of my hotspot data.

Since moving from the suburbs, we obviously had to cut back on our data usage - but that was part of the reason I decided to move out to a rural area. To unplug a little bit more.

We obviously can't watch 12 hours of Netflix, or Hulu a day. But we don't watch that shit anyway.

I do have satellite TV, which suits my limited need to veg out. Its only 60 bucks a month. But, our ATT bill is around 350 bucks a month now. It's kind of a wash, because before our TV/internet bill was around 200 a month and our celll phones were 200 a month. Our bill has about a net increase of 10 bucks.

Hope this helps. It took me a month to figure the best plan that worked for us.

NOTE: not shilling for ATT. Verizon probably has similar plans. We chose ATT because they have the closest cell tower to our property, thus giving us a stronger signal. Find out what tower is closest to you, and see what kind of plans they offer.
